title: Kinship Explorer
description: A family tree centered on You, with Dad's side and Mom's side, that shows the single English word for each of nine relatives next to the term many families use in Hindi-Urdu, Bangla, Punjabi, Tamil and Sinhala, in original script with a respelling. Notes mark where usage varies by family, religion or region.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: South Asian cultures
Family and kinship
Kinship terms
South Asian languages
Sociology
publisher: Roots & Rivers: An Interactive Guide to South Asian Cultures for High School Students
audience: Students, Educators, South Asian student club leaders
learningObjectives: Compare the kinship terms for nine relatives across Hindi-Urdu, Bangla, Punjabi, Tamil and Sinhala.
Explain why many South Asian languages use separate words for relatives on the father's side and the mother's side.
Identify where kinship terms mark age (older and younger relatives) and where usage varies by family, religion or region.
prerequisites: Knowing the English words for close relatives (parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles)
Awareness that South Asian languages use different scripts (Chapter 6)
keyQuestions: Why does English use one word, uncle, for relatives that many South Asian languages name separately?
Which languages split grandparents by side, and which use one word for both?
Why do Tamil and Sinhala call a father's older brother big father?
misconceptions: Mama means mother in every South Asian language.
Every speaker of a language uses the same kinship words.
South Asian languages simply have more words for the same relatives, with no pattern behind them.
controls: Color Dad's side and Mom's side checkbox
Click or tap a relative in the tree
dataSources: Wiktionary entries for each Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, Punjabi, Tamil and Sinhalese term (see logs/13-factcheck.md): https://en.wiktionary.org/
